stories.titleZh: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?

comments.author: bitwizeshift
comments.textRawHtml:
I’m surprised I haven’t see anyone say this yet, but I don’t let the LLM design the code at all, I let it implement a design I have created.

By that I mean that, rather than let the LLM do the entire structure, I take the time to create the full hierarchy of abstractions and actors that I want my code to do. I decide, at the UML level, how abstractions will sit and interact — and then I make the LLM implement those gaps.

The key thing here is that, by doing this, I DO know how the code works. I may not know how each unit is implemented, but I know each unit’s responsibilities and how they interact with one another. I’ve found that LLMs are HORRIBLE at writing decent abstractions, regardless of how much prompting and skills I’ve given it. It will always get the job done, but it will often be unmaintainable and require bigger and heavier refactors as I introduce more and more requirement changes.

But by flexing my basic design skills, I don’t have those issues. Future refactoring fit into easy abstractions that I’ve designed. And by documenting it up front, I also have what becomes a living document on how this work will turn out.

It takes a few hours up front to plan ahead, but it makes the LLMs job easier and use less tokens, and it makes the code better long term. I don’t care if one unit is suboptimal, as long as the abstraction is right — because at worst I can change an implementation for a better one later.

The key thing here is that, by doing this, I DO know how the code works. I may not know how each unit is implemented, but I know each unit’s responsibilities and how they interact with one another. I’ve found that LLMs are HORRIBLE at writing decent abstractions, regardless of how much prompting and skills I’ve given it. It will always get the job done, but it will often be unmaintainable and require bigger and heavier refactors as I introduce more and more requirement changes.

But by flexing my basic design skills, I don’t have those issues. Future refactoring fit into easy abstractions that I’ve designed. And by documenting it up front, I also have what becomes a living document on how this work will turn out.

It takes a few hours up front to plan ahead, but it makes the LLMs job easier and use less tokens, and it makes the code better long term. I don’t care if one unit is suboptimal, as long as the abstraction is right — because at worst I can change an implementation for a better one later.

children.author: davepeck
children.textRawHtml:
A friend of mine sometimes jokes that code is “fractally busted” when it’s wrong at every level, from single lines all the way up to the design of the system’s main interfaces.

That’s also roughly what I find after a long English-only session with a coding agent. Our conversation covers a lot of ground... and leaves out details at every level. When I look at what got built, the misunderstandings are fractal too.

I agree it’s important to design it yourself, but UML is only one level. Lately I’ve been using a scratch Python file (or even a scratch repo) that Claude and I both edit. Never mind that I’m writing Rust. Python reads like pseudocode, and pass and ... (Ellipsis) let me skip whatever I don’t care about. At any level where I do care, I can say exactly what a method’s signature should look like, what fields a domain model should have, or how it should maintain key invariants. Everywhere else I leave an ellipsis, maybe a docstring, and let the agent decide.

It works both ways: I ask the agent to sketch the current system in Python, with some details elided and others spelled out. Then I edit the sketch and have the agent push the changes back into the much bigger Rust+Tauri app.

Time will tell whether this approach has legs, but when I want to be precise, I find it sometimes pays to just write some code.

children.author: stickfigure
children.textRawHtml:
I don't have this experience at all. My workflow is:

* Bite sized jobs, about what you would expect for a traditional user story.

* 10-15 minutes discussing the implementation. It's almost the exact same conversation I would have with a human engineer. I'm almost entirely asking questions - "How would you do Xyz? What about this problem? What about that problem?"

* At the end of the conversation, both the AI and I have a good understanding of the problem and the solution.

* I say "do it".

* There are occasions when I don't fully understand what it wants to do. I'll tell it to do the work, then we discuss it afterwards. Sometimes we change things, sometimes I just need to see the code to understand.

* It doesn't commit code. I do.

This has been really effective for me, easily 10X'd or more my pace of development. Sometimes I have to ask for a lot of rework and sometimes it one-shots it. But I never ship something I don't understand and it always feels like "my" code. Very satisfying. More satisfying than typing it all out; the typing was never the fun part of programming.

children.author: orthogonal_cube
children.textRawHtml:
Reverse-engineering was seen as a challenging hobby where people would deeply collaborate to decipher machine language. People got to know each other pretty well like they were good neighbors thanks to the process. Questions would get asked about patterns people couldn’t resolve on their own which gave opportunities for others to pitch in or relay knowledge. A network would get established.

Now a vibecoded tool gets introduced and it eliminates both the challenge and the need to collaborate. There’s no longer any bragging rights, learning hand-in-hand, pride in completing a project started months ago, nor competition to see how fast someone can complete a project. A tool is now available to all and does the work for them.

To your point, there’s no reason the introduction of the new tools won’t bring people together. The reverse-engineering communities will probably undergo an identity crisis with an exodus of participants and the creation of a new type of challenge. Those who were in it for collaborative work will probably leave and not return. Those who just enjoyed witnessing the end results might stay to discuss and learn from what the tools produce. The discussion content would be different and may draw in a completely different crowd.

I mean, if the introduction of Excel made accounting less tedious by completing previously-manual actions and somehow resulted in a massive global community which holds an annual competition for complex workbook design, then perhaps reverse engineering communities won’t vanish overnight as feared. Time will tell.

Given how expensive this computation would have been in 1997, it makes perfect sense they'd taken months, but even if we assume they tried all timestamps of 1997 and selected arbitrarily among the first 16 viable candidate of any timestamp, that's just ~30 bits of freedom.

comments.author: antasvara
comments.textRawHtml:
Nathan Fielder is pretty well-known for his work in The Rehearsal and Nathan for You. Nathan for You resides in the docu-comedy genre, where you take advantage of real people's reactions to absurd situations for comedic effect. Other examples are things like Kitchen Nightmares (where Gordon Ramsey goes into real restaurants and "fixes" them). It's a well-done version of the idea, but not revolutionary IMO.

The Rehearsal, however, extends the idea further. In that show, he helps real people "rehearse" for hard conversations. It involves Fielder building extravagant sets and having absurdly detailed set-ups with multiple actors, then running the conversation multiple times. What makes this "different" is that now the real person is partially in on it? Like, they know that they're on a set. They know that this is a simulation. So the show is more "meta" than previous entries in the genre, opening up other avenues for humour.

I say this because You Can See Everything is best understood as a further extension of those projects. Even the name indicates this, because by nature of a documentary, you can't see everything. You have a real person in Elizabeth Holmes, being interviewed by a person in Fielder that's known for his stunts taking advantage of "real people," where he watches fictionalized versions of Holmes with Holmes herself? Viewed in light of his previous projects, this feels like an extension of them.

But even with that, I think the setup does allow you to see something real in Holmes. She also knows how people "want" to see her! So there's also a sort of meta-narrative there too, where you know Holmes is on her best behavior to try and dispel the narrative from those fictionalized TV characterizations. The fact that she comes off poorly in the documentary says something, even accounting for the fact that Fielder is trying to sell a narrative.

It's a real mind game, but I think it's representative of Holmes because of that. She is going to jail for a fraud that amounts to a similar sort of mind game, she agrees to a documentary to show herself differently, but that documentary is also a mind game. Wild stuff.

children.textRawHtml:
The fun thing is: I don't think this will change that much with AI in the mix ;)

Shitty devs without AI are slowly building BS that wants to be cleaned up.

Shitty devs with AI are much more fasterly building BS that wants to be cleaned up.

I have a similar experience as yours, just add another 10-ish years to the timeline. Literally my first job out of uni, I got to work on a legacy code base that was another 15 years older than that which had a ton of reports all built differently over time with slight variations in both code and end user output that really all wanted to be "the same" both on the code and end user side. So I slowly but surely, one user/PM requested change at a time would build out a common layer of abstractions and shared code that both made the code shared and easier to maintain (great for me!) and consistent for users (great for the PM/users).

Heck, I built a rudimentary TransactSQL parser that'd output stored procedure call graphs to graphviz and then I printed it and hung it on the wall to get through all this and having an LLM to just make a mermaid out of this in 5-ish minutes would definitively have been faster than I was ;)

With an LLM all of that would just have been faster to do but still worthwhile and useful on both levels. I.e. both code abstraction/reuse and PM/user level. Similarly there was a report that one of the devs had to actually run manually and it took him a full week, so users that wanted the report would only request it once a year-ish. When I was asked to learn how to run it from him I was appalled and just took that week to put it into a script that we ran and emailed the report out once a month automatically. They ran that report manually like that for like 10 years prior to that :mindblown:

None of this is an "AI thing". It's a good dev vs. not so good dev thing. And none of it really has to do with coding as in "writing source code" as much as "solving problems for humans" somehow and the "language" you do that in changes over time. If you're the guy that's tied up with the particular language: yeah LLMs are gonna eat your lunch. If you're the problem solver type that uses whatever tools they have available, you're still in demand.

The leak was for something called 'OpenCode Console', which is distinct and separate from the OpenCode coding agent. If you're just using the coding agent, you're not affected. 'OpenCode Console' is a service that is similar to OpenRouter, but is much less widely used.

Today is a bad day for people using 'OpenCode Console'. But most people, probably the vast majority of OpenCode users who are reading this, are not using 'OpenCode Console'.

children.author: jerieljan
children.textRawHtml:
Yeah, it's very confusing especially if you're not in the loop and their docs were only updated recently and was confusing during the v1 -> v2 transition weeks / months ago.

So far, "OpenCode" has gone through several possible definitions:

- OpenCode Terminal / CLI - This is what you get normally. Runs a service in the background and the CLI is your interface.

- OpenCode Desktop - Instead of a CLI, you get a desktop interface.

Most users usually stop here. You just install the app and you connect wherever.

So there's the services where they both make money and make things easier for users:

- OpenCode Console - Basically the serving platform for both Zen and Go, and has expanded to a hosted inference gateway and somewhat similar to OpenRouter or a managed LiteLLM. Has the option to BYOK if you have existing AI platform accounts so it charges those instead of Zen, and that's what got compromised.

- OpenCode Zen - the API service they host if you want to get access to providers but don't want to pay individually per API platform. Similar to OpenRouter. I noticed they're kinda slowly dropping the Zen moniker.

- OpenCode Go - the subscription service that they host that features open weight models and select low-cost models from frontier labs. Has different policies when it comes to privacy and retention compared to Zen.

- OpenCode Black - a limited-time, limited access subscription service that grants access to frontier models. Not sure if this is still alive or not.
